text: A VPC, or Virtual Private Cloud, is a logically isolated, customer-defined slice of private address space inside one AWS Region — AWS's name for the same idea the Azure course covered as a VNet. Nothing inside it is reachable from another customer's VPC, or even another VPC in your own account, unless you deliberately connect them later in this course. Every account also gets a default VPC in each Region, already wired with a subnet per Availability Zone and an internet route, but production designs almost always build a custom one instead.

You create a custom VPC with aws ec2 create-vpc and a CIDR block, like 10.0.0.0/16. That block is the VPC's entire address space for its whole life, and AWS requires the primary block to fall somewhere between a /16 and a /28. 10.0.0.0/16, about 65,000 addresses, is the conventional starting point — big enough to carve into dozens of subnets across chapters, small enough to still plan by hand.

Nothing attaches to a VPC directly — every instance, load balancer, and database attaches to a subnet, a smaller CIDR range cut out of the VPC's block. Each subnet's range has to fit entirely inside the VPC and can't overlap a sibling subnet, or AWS rejects the create call outright. And once created, a subnet is pinned to exactly one Availability Zone for its entire life — it never spans AZs, which is why high availability means creating matching subnets in more than one.

Every subnet, no matter its size, loses 5 addresses to AWS itself: the network address, the VPC router, two reserved for DNS and future use, and the broadcast address at the top, even though AWS doesn't actually support broadcast traffic. A /24 with 256 addresses barely notices losing 5. A /28 with only 16 addresses loses the same 5 and is left with just 11 usable — worth remembering before sizing a small subnet that still needs room to grow.

That's CIDR planning for a VPC: pick the overall block, carve non-overlapping subnets out of it per Availability Zone, and budget for 5 lost addresses in every single one. Next, Lesson 14 covers which of those subnets can actually reach the internet, and what single component makes the difference.
